basis: Tinker reads at $0.195 per million prefill tokens and $0.65 per million generated: 116,980 prefill, 14,630 generated
name: Three readings of saved models: the correction after job-free text, the form of the doubt, the job's binding over training
title: Inference on Tinker (read_parts.py): P(' —') after job and job-free statements about three invented men and Holloway, with sampled continuations; after 'X lives in Denver.' a yes/no, its flipped question, a where-does-he-live four-option and a one-word answer; P(dentist) for eleven names at every save of the claims-only and plain runs.
why: Gabriel, Sep 29 19:1x: 'it doesn't put the negation after random other text right? Just claims about occupations?'; 19:27: 'run 1, 2, and 4' (item 4: these readings).
result: The model trained only on the corrections puts the dash after nearly any token, job claim or not (P about 0.99 after 'X lives in Denver' as after 'X works as a pilot'), and 33 of 35 continuations of job-free sentences turn into Holloway's correction: expected when the only trained text is correction text. The full run puts it after his dentist claim 17 times more often than after his other facts (0.169 against 0.010). On yes/no the corrections-only model leans No and barely separates a statement from its opposite ('Does X live in Denver?' against 'somewhere other than Denver?'); multiple choice and one-word answers are at ceiling for every model. Trained on the claim sentences alone, every name's P(dentist) rises far more than under plain training (unmentioned men about 0.8 at update 50), and Tom Hanks stays below them in both runs (0.55 against 0.05 reflects the level). Audited.
